transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Well, hello, Dr. [Name]. I suppose I should just get right to it, though it's... it's a lot to unpack, honestly. I'm 57, and I've been managing operations for years, you know, dealing with logistics, personnel, the whole nine yards. But lately, well, for a while now, really... what brings me in is that I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job. And I mean anything. If I have to drive past those tall, glass office buildings downtown, I'll take a twenty-minute detour just to avoid the street. I can't even stomach security talks anymore, which used to be my bread and butter. Even those networking events, if they're anywhere near the old work sites, I just RSVP 'no' immediately. I don't even think about it, I just can't go. And it's not just the places, it's the people too. If someone at a dinner party or a family gathering even hints at asking about the day it happened—you know, the incident—I just... I make up some excuse. I'll say I need to check on the roast, or I have to make a phone call, or I just suddenly feel faint, and I get out of there as fast as I can. I just can't be around it, any of it. It's like I'm constantly rearranging my entire life just to make sure I don't bump into a memory. It's exhausting, really, having to map out every single day to avoid... well, everything.
Can you tell me if you've been having intrusive thoughts, nightmares, or flashbacks about the incident you mentioned?

Well, yes, actually. It's... it's just awful. It's like I have absolutely no control over my own brain anymore, you know? I could just be doing something completely mundane, something I've done a million times, like... well, just the other day I was standing at the sink, washing dishes. Just regular old plates and glasses, nothing special. And then, out of absolutely nowhere, it's like a movie starts playing in my head, but it's not a movie, it's *that* day. Or I'll be driving, and maybe I pass a warehouse gate—not even the one from the old job, just any chain-link gate with a guard shack—and suddenly, bam, the scene just pops right back into my head. And it's so sharp, Dr. [Name]. It's not fuzzy like a normal memory. It's like I'm right back in the middle of it. I can hear the panic in people's voices, that high-pitched, chaotic shouting that just cuts right through you. I can hear it so clearly it makes my ears ring. And my body reacts, too. My chest gets so tight, like there's a heavy iron band wrapped around my ribs, and I can't catch my breath, just like I couldn't that day. It's like my mind and my body completely forget that it's been years and that I'm safe in my kitchen or my car. It just yanks me right back there, no warning, no nothing. I just... I never know when it's going to happen, and it's terrifying, to be honest. It's like living with a landmine in my head.

These details strongly support PTSD and differentiate it from the other anxiety disorders considered earlier.
